expression: to fall behind with one's studies
usage: Used when someone is not keeping up with the required pace of their course due to illness, work, or lack of time.
example_sentences: I’ve been so busy with my part-time job that I’m starting to fall behind with my studies.
If you miss too many lectures, you will inevitably fall behind with your studies.
She had to take a week off to recover, so she’s currently falling behind with her studies.
It’s very easy to fall behind with your studies if you don't manage your time effectively.
After falling behind with my studies last term, I’ve decided to hire a private tutor.
opposites: to stay on top of one's work
native_notes: We use this specifically for academic progress. 'Lag behind' is more general and can apply to anything, whereas 'fall behind with studies' is the go-to academic phrasing.

usage: Used when students stay awake all night to study or finish an assignment before a deadline.
example_sentences: I had to pull an all-nighter to finish my final dissertation before the deadline.
Pulling an all-nighter is never a good idea as you won't be sharp for the exam.
Most university students have pulled an all-nighter at least once in their life.
She was exhausted after pulling an all-nighter to prepare for the chemistry test.
If you plan your time better, you won't need to pull an all-nighter.
native_notes: This is very common among students. 'Burn the midnight oil' is a bit more formal/idiomatic, while 'pull an all-nighter' is standard student slang.

usage: Used when someone needs to start studying seriously or begin an intensive session of revision.
alternatives: to get down to some serious studying
example_sentences: I need to hit the books this weekend because my final exams are just around the corner.
No more parties for me—it's time to hit the books.
He went to the library to hit the books for his upcoming history seminar.
If you want to pass this module, you’d better start hitting the books now.
After a long break, it was hard to hit the books again.
native_notes: It implies a sudden start to serious work. It sounds more active and determined than simply 'studying'.

usage: Used when describing an exam or task that was extremely easy for someone to complete.
alternatives: to find something a walk in the park
example_sentences: Because she had prepared so well, she was able to breeze through the final interview.
He’s so gifted at mathematics that he breezed through the exam in under an hour.
Don't assume you'll breeze through the course; it’s actually quite challenging.
She breezed through the presentation as if she had been practicing for weeks.
I was worried about the history paper, but I managed to breeze through it.
native_notes: Implies effortless success. Use this when the outcome was never in doubt due to the person's high ability.

usage: Used in academic or professional contexts to highlight the value of practical work over mere theory.
example_sentences: The internship program allows students to gain hands-on experience in the field of engineering.
Theoretical knowledge is useful, but nothing beats the value of gaining hands-on experience.
Our curriculum is designed to help students gain hands-on experience before they graduate.
She decided to take a gap year to gain hands-on experience in wildlife conservation.
Employers are increasingly looking for graduates who have gained hands-on experience during their studies.
native_notes: Crucial phrase for IELTS Writing Task 2 when discussing education vs. employment. It sounds much more professional than 'doing practical work'.

expression: to fall behind with your studies
usage: Used when a student fails to keep up with the pace of their coursework or assignments.
example_sentences: I was ill for a week, so I've really fallen behind with my studies.
It is very easy to fall behind with your studies if you don't manage your time well.
She had to drop a module because she was falling behind with her studies.
If you fall behind with your studies, talk to your tutor as soon as possible.
The heavy workload meant that many students started to fall behind with their studies.
native_notes: We often use 'with' here, though 'in' is sometimes heard in US English. In British English, 'fall behind with' is standard.

usage: Used to describe completing a task or an exam very easily and successfully.
alternatives: find it a piece of cake
example_sentences: Because she had studied so hard, she managed to breeze through the final exam.
I thought the test would be difficult, but I actually breezed through it.
He breezed through the presentation as if he had been practising for weeks.
She didn't even sweat; she just breezed through the assessment.
Most students found the module hard, but he breezed through the assignments.
native_notes: ‘Breeze through’ implies that the process was not just successful, but remarkably simple and smooth.

usage: Used when someone passes a test or succeeds, but only just, usually by a very small margin.
alternatives: to pass by the skin of one's teeth
example_sentences: I didn't prepare well enough, so I only managed to scrape through the maths exam.
He scraped through the interview, but he didn't feel very confident about the job.
If you don't attend the tutorials, you'll be lucky to scrape through the course.
She scraped through the language proficiency test with the minimum required score.
He had no interest in the subject and only scraped through with a passing grade.
native_notes: The focus is on the narrowness of the success. It is not a positive term, but it implies a result was achieved.

usage: Used when a student fails to keep up with the pace of a course or class due to absence or difficulty.
example_sentences: If you miss too many lectures, you will quickly fall behind with your coursework.
I’ve been sick for a week, so I’m really falling behind in my maths class.
He had to take extra lessons to catch up because he fell behind last semester.
It's hard not to fall behind when the curriculum moves this fast.
She didn't want to fall behind, so she spent the whole weekend studying.
native_notes: Often used with prepositions 'in' (for a subject) or 'with' (for assignments).

usage: Used to describe passing an exam or finishing a course with little to no effort.
example_sentences: She studied so hard that she managed to sail through her final examinations.
Because of his experience, he sailed through the interview process.
Most students found the test difficult, but Sarah sailed through it without any issues.
I thought the chemistry module would be tough, but I sailed through it.
Don't expect to sail through this course without doing any reading.
native_notes: Suggests that the task was much easier than expected.

usage: Used when keeping pace with the workload or the level of difficulty in a classroom setting.
example_sentences: I'm finding it difficult to keep up with all the reading assignments.
If you work consistently, you'll have no trouble keeping up with the class.
The professor speaks so quickly that it's hard to keep up with his lecture notes.
She is really smart and has no problem keeping up with the advanced students.
How do you manage to keep up with all your deadlines?
native_notes: Can also be used in business/social contexts, not just education.

usage: Used when starting to understand a complicated subject or a new method of study.
grammar_pattern: Subject + get(s) to grips with + noun/V-ing
example_sentences: It took me a while to get to grips with the new research methodology.
Once you get to grips with the basic concepts, the rest of the course is straightforward.
The seminar helped us get to grips with the complexities of economic policy.
She is finally getting to grips with how to use the laboratory equipment.
I am still trying to get to grips with these statistical software tools.
collocations: get to grips with a problem
get to grips with new ideas
native_notes: Suggests that the topic was initially difficult or challenging.

uzbek: osonlik bilan o'tib ketmoq, qiyinchiliksiz uddalamoq
usage: Used to describe completing a task, exam, or course with very little effort or difficulty.
example_sentences: Because she had studied so much, she cruised through the final exam.
Some students find the first year of university easy and cruise through their assignments.
I expected the chemistry test to be difficult, but I actually cruised through it.
He didn't really prepare, but he still managed to cruise through the presentation.
Don't assume you will cruise through the course; the later modules are quite challenging.
native_notes: Similar to 'breeze through'. It suggests that the person was well-prepared or the task was surprisingly simple.

uzbek: talab darajasida bo'lmaslik, kutilgan natijani bermaslik
usage: Used when exam results, grades, or academic performance fail to meet the required standard or expectations.
example_sentences: Unfortunately, his final score fell short of the university's entrance requirement.
The quality of the essay fell short of what the professor expected from a top student.
Many graduates find that their practical skills fall short of the demands of the modern workplace.
If your grades fall short, you may need to consider an alternative course.
The research project fell short of its initial objectives due to a lack of funding.
native_notes: This is often used to sound more professional and less harsh than saying someone 'failed' or 'is bad'.
russian: не находясь на необходимом уровне, не давая ожидаемого результата

expression: to keep up with the workload
usage: Used to describe managing the volume of assignments, reading, and tasks required by a course.
grammar_pattern: Subject + keep up with + the workload
alternatives: to stay on top of things
example_sentences: The medical course is intense, and it's hard to keep up with the workload.
I had to quit my part-time job to keep up with the workload at university.
If you are organized, it is much easier to keep up with the workload.
Many students struggle to keep up with the workload in their final year.
She is excellent at planning her time so she can keep up with the workload.
opposites: to be overwhelmed by the workload
native_notes: Distinguishes between general study habits and the specific volume of tasks ('workload').

usage: Used when talking about learning the essential basics of a subject that will lead to more advanced knowledge later.
grammar_pattern: Subject + set + the foundation + for + noun/V-ing
example_sentences: Primary school is essential to set the foundation for future academic success.
This introductory course helps to set the foundation for more complex topics.
His early interest in mathematics set the foundation for his career in engineering.
We need to set the foundation now, or the project will fail later.
A strong command of grammar sets the foundation for fluent language use.
native_notes: Use this in academic contexts to describe the 'why' something is taught at an early stage.

usage: Used when discussing entry requirements, grading rubrics, or academic standards.
common_mistakes: meet the criterion (when plural is needed)
example_sentences: To get into the university, you must meet the criteria set by the admissions board.
His essay failed to meet the criteria for a top-grade assignment.
Many applicants do not meet the criteria for this specific scholarship.
We need to ensure that our research methods meet the criteria for publication.
The project met all the criteria required for academic excellence.
native_notes: Note that 'criteria' is plural; 'criterion' is the singular form. Never use 'criterias'.

usage: Used when someone achieves an excellent score or succeeds in a challenge with high merit.
example_sentences: She was nervous about the physics paper, but she passed with flying colours.
If you study consistently, I’m sure you’ll pass the IELTS with flying colours.
He managed to pass his driving test with flying colours on the first attempt.
The students who attended all tutorials passed the module with flying colours.
I didn't expect to pass with flying colours given how difficult the questions were.
collocations: expect to pass with flying colours
native_notes: Note the British spelling 'colours'. It suggests success with a significant margin.

usage: Used when an exam is surprisingly easy or when a student finds the material very manageable.
alternatives: to find it a walk in the park
example_sentences: Because I had revised the material thoroughly, I sailed through the exam.
The maths paper was so straightforward that most students sailed through it.
I was worried about the interview, but I sailed through it without any issues.
Some students seem to sail through exams, while others have to struggle.
After weeks of practice, I sailed through the practical component of the course.
native_notes: Implies effortless success. Use this to describe exams that were unexpectedly easy.

usage: Standard term used when a student leaves university or college before completing their degree.
example_sentences: It's a shame that he decided to drop out of university in his final year.
The tuition fees were so high that many students were forced to drop out of the course.
She dropped out of medical school to pursue a career in music.
Not everyone who starts a degree finishes it; drop-out rates are actually quite high.
He felt uninspired and eventually chose to drop out of his economics programme.
native_notes: Note the hyphenated form 'drop-out' (noun) vs the phrasal verb 'drop out' (verb).
